items.title: EA is shutting down BioWare
items.summary: Article URL: https://www.theverge.com/games/1015647/ea-is-shutting-down-bioware Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50184586 Points: 391 # Comments: 239
items.content:
Amid a reported 400 job cuts, the legendary studio is closing.

BioWare, the legendary studio behind RPGs like Mass Effect , Dragon Age , and Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic , is shutting down, the company confirmed in a statement . Alongside the closure, Electronic Arts has chosen not to continue development on the next Mass Effect game that was in the works, according to an announcement sent to EA staff .

The company is also laying off around 400 staffers, Bloomberg reports , including around 50 at BioWare. The changes follow EA being taken private by an investor group led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund, Silver Lake, and Affinity Partners in a $55 billion deal that closed in August . Other major gaming companies have made sweeping changes this year as well, including Xbox’s “reset” that will include 3,200 cuts , Bungie’s “significant” layoffs , and Fortnite maker Epic Games laying off over 1,000 staff .

“BioWare is a legendary studio that helped define the role-playing genre, and we do not take this decision lightly,” Cam Weber, EA president and chief studios officer, and David Tinson, EA president and COO, said in the announcement.

Here is the full message that BioWare shared on social media:

For more than 30 years, BioWare has been more than a studio. It has been a home for storytellers, developers, and the players who brought our worlds to life.

Baldur’s Gate. Neverwinter Nights. Star Wars: Knights of the Old Republic. Dragon Age. Mass Effect. Anthem.

Now, after more than three decades of shared adventures, BioWare is closing and early development on the next Mass Effect project is ending.

There is nothing easy about writing those words. Our focus right now is on our incredibly talented team who put their hearts into these games, and supporting one another through this transition.

What generations of BioWare built together is something to celebrate and remember. These games became so much more because you played them, debated your choices, fell in love with the characters, and made these worlds your own.

From all of us at BioWare, thank you for being the most meaningful part of our story.

While the end of BioWare will shock many gamers who fondly remember its hits, the company hasn’t been as successful in recent years. 2017’s Mass Effect: Andromeda was widely seen as a misstep for that franchise, it took a big bet on live service games in 2019 with Anthem that didn’t pan out , and EA laid off some BioWare staff in 2025 after Dragon Age: The Veilguard missed sales expectations .

There is no word yet on the fate of Amazon’s Mass Effect TV series. Last we heard , Amazon’s head of TV was close to giving it the green light, but had reportedly requested rewrites to make the show “more appealing to non-gamers.” Amazon didn’t immediately reply to a request for comment. EA spokesperson Justin Higgs said he had “Nothing to share on that at this point.”

In EA’s company-wide announcement, Weber and Tinson outlined several other projects in development and changes to EA’s roadmap. The executives say that Respawn and DICE will be collaborating on “a future project,” which Bloomberg says is “likely” a new Star Wars: Battlefront game. The company is still working Marvel’s Iron Man and a new Star Wars Jedi title. EA is making a “brand-new, social-first open-world experience” football game that it calls “Project Gridiron” and is also in pre-production on a new Fight Night boxing title ( which was teased yesterday ). For The Sims , the company is pausing development on “Project Lotus” and focusing on “Project Evergreen.” And for its live-service Skate , EA is “making changes to the studio” to “deliver on a very clear roadmap for our community.”

Here is the full message from Weber and Tinson at Electronic Arts:

Through every major moment we’ve faced as a company, your commitment to creating awesome games and experiences for our players continues to be impressive. Together, we’ve built epic worlds and global communities that are part of the lives of hundreds of millions of people.

Today, we’re the number one publisher in Western HD gaming. That’s an extraordinary position to lead from, and one we should be proud of. Yet our industry is changing quickly. Players have more choices than ever for their time and attention, competition is intensifying, and some of our biggest opportunities for growth are beyond the markets, platforms, and business models where EA has traditionally been the strongest.

That’s why, over the past several months, we’ve taken a hard look at our business, how we operate, and what it will take to lead in this next era of interactive entertainment. We’ve challenged assumptions, confronted hard realities, imagined new possibilities, and made deliberate choices in order to deliver exceptional experiences for our players and to drive sustained growth.

We believe our best creative work happens when we’re clear about what matters most for our players and give our teams the freedom to move quickly. So, we’re concentrating our teams, technology, and investment behind these three strategic priorities.

These priorities will bring clarity and focus to your work every day, and so will the way we work. We’ve spent time listening to teams about what’s working, what’s getting in the way, and what you need to do your best work. The feedback was consistent: you want clearer priorities, faster decisions, and teams that work more closely together. We’ve already begun simplifying how we work so we can spend more time creating and innovating for our players.

Across our portfolio, we’re making deliberate choices to align talent and investments where we see the greatest opportunities for players and long-term growth.

items.title: This Startup Is All In on Recursive Self-Improvement. Its Latest Model Is Scary Good
items.summary: Recursive makes the case that the benefits of using AI to build AI outweigh the risks.
items.content:
For the past few days I’ve been testing an impressive open-weight AI coding model called Flint. It suggests that fully recursive self-improvement , or RSI—an exciting and controversial approach that uses AI to build AI—is getting closer.

Flint is the first offering from Recursive, a company that aims to use RSI to advance both AI itself and other areas of science using AI . “Nearly every aspect of the entire model pipeline was actually done and improved upon by AI,” Recursive CEO and cofounder Richard Socher told me.

Socher says his company used its recursive AI system, dubbed the Eureka Machine, to automate most elements of the model’s development. This enabled a company with a handful of researchers to build a world-class model in just a few months, he says.

Socher told me that the Eureka Machine devised a number of innovations, including a new way of training the base model, new model architectures, and code optimized for specific silicon chips. Recursive shared benchmark scores that suggest Flint outperforms other models of similar size and architecture on coding tasks.

AI is already widely used to help build, test, and improve AI thanks to its amazing coding skills. This can speed up the process of refining a model and testing new ideas without the need for as much input from humans.

It is also possible to create a loop through which AI decides what improvements to make and then begins another round of improvement. For the moment this technique is limited, but if AI can contribute to every aspect of model development, then the process could theoretically continue indefinitely.

Some experts worry that letting AI improve itself in this manner could ultimately lead to disaster . These doomsayers claim that AI capable of improving indefinitely could escape human control and might decide that humans are an impediment to its goals.

Those concerns gained wider notice this September when a researcher quit Anthropic and warned that advances in AI, including recursive self-improvement, could lead to human extinction within a few years—a concern then echoed by a number of other experts. The idea of RSI has become so controversial that several bills in Congress propose to ban it.

Recursive sees these fears as more sci-fi than reality and believes legislation to prevent RSI is an unnecessary impediment to progress.

Socher says Flint was built using a system incapable of escaping human control. He says the goal is for the Eureka Machine itself to achieve full recursive self-improvement, but this would still be overseen by humans who could stop the process if it goes awry. “We hope that this shows people that indeed we have all the steps in place” to build such a system, he says.

Recursive has raised $650 million at a $4.65 billion valuation from Google Ventures, Greycroft, Nvidia, and AMD Ventures. Socher was previously the chief scientist at Salesforce, and his cofounders include Jeff Clune, a professor at the University of British Columbia who researches ways of building AI systems capable of learning indefinitely.

I must say I am impressed with Flint. I tested it on a Mac with 48 GB of RAM—a healthy amount but only enough to run a modest-size AI model like Flint, which has 40 billion parameters. The biggest models out there have several trillions of parameters, and they can only run on racks of industrial servers.

I used Flint to build a bunch of programs and found it to be both fast and very capable. In my experience, models of this size can be annoyingly error-prone or slow compared to Claude or Codex, but Flint nailed my coding requests every time. I used it to create a command line to-do list, then tried having it build a program that scours the web for interesting research related to recursive self-improvement. I also had Flint whip up a simple website that explains how RSI works. You can see that here .

It’s unclear how much progress other US labs have made chasing recursive self-improvement, but some published work suggests fully recursive systems are already feasible. A team from Microsoft, Carnegie Mellon University, and the University of Virginia recently published work, for instance, showing how an AI coding agent can recursively improve itself by modifying the software harness that turns reasoning into useful action and its own model’s weights.

Perhaps there are risks to full RSI if you are close to building a godlike intelligence, but for the time being it seems like a very promising way to improve your own AI models. This is something I’ve dabbled with in previous editions of AI Lab .

Indeed, Socher says the approach used to build Flint could make cutting-edge AI more accessible. “It's the only way this very small team can produce a model that's actually better than any other model in its class,” he told me. “This will hopefully show people that [recursive self-improvement] is actually quite nice and will benefit a lot of people.”

items.title: The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure
items.summary: We moved a copy of 99.99999% of GitHub's repositories to Azure. Here's how per-reference quorums will bring over the rest, and how object storage lets reads scale independently. The post The bridge to agent-scale Git infrastructure appeared first on The GitHub Blog .
items.content:
Over the past year, while Git traffic grew exponentially, 99.99999% of the Git repositories on GitHub began living in two places at once: our own data centers and Azure. The rest are among the busiest on the platform, and they’re held back by just one thing: a 25ms round trip.

In an earlier blog post , we laid out the two principles behind our next-generation storage architecture:

In this post, we’ll look at the immediate bridge between our old design and our new one. We’ll talk about how a change to the way our quorum serializes writes gets the busiest repositories into Azure, and how that same step opens the door to replicas that keep no persistent state of their own.

The timing and shape of the move were driven by the agentic shift: rapidly growing traffic, a hard ceiling on the power capacity of our data centers and the surrounding geographical region, and physical supply chain constraints. At the beginning of our migration, the remaining capacity with all possible expansion gave us enough time to migrate safely, but not enough to do it slowly.

While we had prototyped new architectural approaches for scaling Git on cloud infrastructure, changing the storage architecture and the hosting platform at the same time, under that growth, carried too much risk. Given our scale and how critical the service is to the community, we needed to sequence the work carefully: move the data first, then evolve the architecture once it arrived.

Git operations are a Tier 0 service: they’re a core function of GitHub, and nearly everything in GitHub depends on the repository data. That meant the data, services, and every dependency had to move first. The first copy of a repository landed in Azure’s Central US region in August 2025. Today, most repositories have two of their five replicas in Azure, and Azure serves about half of Git traffic. For most of that time, Azure absorbed our growth while our own data centers held steady.

During the migration, traffic follows the data. Most repositories have five replicas to balance durability, availability, and scale. To minimize read latency, Spokes uses preferential routing to direct traffic to a replica in the same region and availability zone as the request. As replicas move to Azure, the share of the traffic that can be served from Azure grows with each one, until the last replica arrives and the old region stops receiving requests entirely. Every repository goes through this process:

So, what about the remaining 0.00001% of repositories?

In our current architecture, a repository hosted in more than one region has a lower write throughput ceiling. Spokes’ quorum only needs a majority to commit a write, but it waits for every healthy replica to respond (up to a timeout) before moving on, so slow replicas delay every write rather than falling behind. In practice, that means the slowest healthy replica sets the latency of every write, and because each write holds a repository-wide lock until it commits, it also sets the throughput ceiling. Once a replica lives in the target Azure region, it’s about 1,000 miles from our data centers, making each network round trip around 25ms, and a write requires multiple round trips. A repository already near its throughput ceiling can’t absorb that on every serialized write; it would fall further behind with every push.

This is where our first principle, minimizing coordination, comes into play. Specifically for this case: don’t serialize what doesn’t need to be. Git’s consistency requirements apply to each reference individually. Once the server accepts an update to a reference, no client should see an older value afterward, only that value or a newer one. That holds whether the update is a fast-forward, a force push, or a delete. But in most cases, updates to different references don’t depend on each other and can be applied independently.

So, we’re changing the scope of the quorum from the whole repository to individual references.

Holding a repository-wide lock for the entire reference update, round trips included, turns the quorum into a single, unordered request queue with one write in flight at a time. Each write in that queue takes as long as the slowest healthy replica. As the write rate grows, so does the queue, and each write waits longer than the one before it.

With per-reference serialization, only writes that contend on a shared reference must wait for each other. In practice, most writes to a repository touch different references—for example, agents and developers pushing to their own branches—so they no longer wait on each other. Each write still experiences the cross-region latency but writes to different references can be in flight at the same time. That removes the single bottleneck on the repository. We can visualize how queueing and timeouts build up by comparing the two approaches side by side under similar load:

These changes raise a repository’s write throughput ceiling roughly in proportion to how many references are being written at once, and get the last remaining repositories into Azure. In internal testing with realistic traffic, writes to different references consistently saw 3–4x higher throughput at lower latency.

Most repositories are heavily read-skewed, with somewhere between 100 and 1,000 reads for every write. Today, reads and writes hit the same replicas, so they compete for the same resources and can’t be scaled independently.

Decoupling storage from compute changes that. Once repository data is durably stored in Azure Blob Storage and updated with each incoming write, we can begin to decouple read traffic from the write quorum, and independently scale the compute needed for each. For example, reads would benefit from far more in-memory cache than we give them today, but that memory is also needed for compaction. Once they’re separated, each gets its own configuration.

items.title: Today's PHP security release, and how we're strengthening security
items.summary: Related ongoing thread: PHP 8.2.35 - https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50180873 (links to more at https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50184935 ) Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50182987 Points: 510 # Comments: 250
items.content:
Earlier today, the PHP project released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35. These releases fix two critical vulnerabilities that, under the right conditions, allow an unauthenticated attacker to execute code on servers running PHP. If you run PHP, it is imperative that you update now. The announcement on php.net contains and references technical details on the vulnerabilities, attack vectors, and instructions on how to update on which systems.

This post isn't about how to update. It's about how these vulnerabilities were found and fixed, what has changed in how PHP security is handled over the past two years, and what we need from the organizations that depend on PHP to keep PHP's security work going.

Both issues sit in parts of PHP that nearly every request touches: memory management and error handling. Their central place in PHP is what made both vulnerabilities serious, and also so hard to fix without breaking compatibility, hurting performance, or forcing changes on the large ecosystem of third-party extensions.

In 2024, PHP underwent its first external security audit in years. The PHP Foundation secured funding from the Sovereign Tech Agency to organize this audit through OSTIF , and it was carried out by Quarkslab . While fixing one of the issues Quarkslab reported, a PHP core developer contracted by the PHP Foundation found the first signs of the OOM problem behind CVE-2026-109618. In 2024, a potential exploit for the OOM problem was theorized, but no concrete vectors were found and other concrete issues with clear impact overshadowed these concerns.

To fix the OOM problem, the PHP security team developed several competing approaches, but each came with its own trade-offs: backward compatibility breaks, new denial-of-service potential, or requiring changes to many third-party extensions which seemed impossible to coordinate. The PHP security team, operating on consensus, struggled to choose between these and feared the repercussions of shipping the wrong choice. Combined with the lack of a known path to remote code execution and the small team of core developers with the necessary deep knowledge of the engine occupied with many responsibilities, this decision process caused work on a fix to stall and restart repeatedly over months. We won't pretend otherwise: the delay was a structural failure, caused by both the security team's decision process and its lack of resources. The security team has since started changing its processes, and that work continues, so that decisions can be made by majority and compromises are encouraged.

Over the last months the way PHP security work is organized has changed considerably. In May 2026, the PHP Foundation created the Ecosystem Security Team , which works alongside the PHP security team on triage, coordination, and hardening. Volker Dusch's work as AI Security Engineer in Residence at the PHP Foundation has significantly improved communication and collaboration between the PHP security team and the Foundation. Alexandre Daubois joined the PHP Foundation in July to help the PHP security team triage, handle, and fix security reports and Daniel Scherzer joined in September to take on hardening work.

Earlier this year, we worked with Alpha-Omega to scan PHP with Anthropic's Claude Mythos. But since the Mythos scan, we have added other tools, including OpenAI's Daybreak Red for validating reports and exploits, alongside sanitizer builds and reproduction environments that match our CI on every platform PHP supports.

The PHP Foundation got the PHP project into the Patch the Planet program, as part of which security firm Calif began an audit of PHP on July 30th, 2026. On August 11th researcher Ryan A at Calif reported an unconditional remote code execution with the same root cause as the OOM problem we had found in 2024. OpenAI independently reported the same root cause on the same day, followed by further attack vectors from OpenAI on September 18th and from Wiz on August 24th. More recently, Trail of Bits has also been auditing PHP. The reports from Calif, OpenAI, and Wiz made the full impact of the OOM problem clear, and from August 11th onward, fixing it became the top priority for all of the PHP Foundation's team working on security. Without the Foundation’s funding it would have been impossible to have multiple people work on this issue full time, eventually through weekends and around the clock to coordinate and communicate with other involved parties.

The growth of AI-assisted research also means the PHP security team receives far more reports than before. As Alexandre Daubois described last week in How the PHP Security Team Handles Your Reports , the team has published 15 CVEs since July 1st and worked through more than 100 reports that turned out to be invalid, duplicates, or not reproducible. AI helps the team validate reports and group reports sharing the same root cause, but a person makes every call and works on every patch.

The coordinated disclosure of these vulnerabilities worked well until 2 days ahead of the targeted release date.

On Tuesday, October 20th, at around 15:00 UTC, the two CVE IDs began circulating on online forums and social media. They came with a wrong release time and a wrong CVSS score of 10.0 (the actual score is 9.2). No technical details leaked. In response, the PHP project brought its pre-announcement forward and published it at 19:30 UTC . It also moved the release from October 22nd, 14:00 UTC, to October 21st, 14:00 UTC. Distributors were still packaging the fix, so releasing immediately would have left many users without an easy way to update. Moving the release forward by one day was the best compromise between acting quickly, giving people time to prepare, and making sure everyone had a simple update path when the vulnerabilities were disclosed.

items.title: The $15 billion ad-powered AI startup your doctor may already be using
items.summary: OpenEvidence is booming despite questions about accuracy and ads.
items.content:
Nearly two-thirds of US doctors are turning to an AI-powered search engine to make patient decisions, propelling a little-known tech startup to a $15 billion valuation while prompting a debate over the future of patient care.

Miami-based OpenEvidence, founded by serial entrepreneur Daniel Nadler in 2022, said that many of America’s 1 million physicians processed more than 42 million prompts last month. Doctors are using the company’s chatbot to scour medical journals and clinical guidelines to help diagnose and treat patients.

The ads-powered platform has grown largely by word of mouth, penetrating a sector where few tools have seen similar traction. “We’re the first viral consumer internet app in healthcare,” Nadler told the FT in an interview.

OpenEvidence has won praise from medical professionals who have found it helped ease workloads, according to interviews with eight senior physicians.

But it faces a nascent threat from large AI companies such as OpenAI and Anthropic, who are making a push into the space. Its growing influence has also prompted scrutiny from researchers concerned over the accuracy of its results, as doctors grow more dependent on an AI tool shaping the course of treatments.

The company’s rapid ascent has attracted nearly $1 billion in investment in the past 18 months, from backers including Andreessen Horowitz, Blackstone, Thrive Capital, and Sequoia. The group raised $250 million in its latest funding round in September at a $15 billion valuation.

OpenEvidence booked $100 million in “ad buys”—a metric that covers current and future advertising commitments—for this year at the end of 2025, according to a person close to the company. The startup is on track to generate between $400 million and $500 million through ads by the end of 2026, the person added.

Credit: OpenEvidence Credit: OpenEvidence

Nadler’s company has penetrated an established market for medical software that was sluggish to incorporate generative AI models. Dutch IT group Wolters Kluwer released an AI version of its leading subscription-based UpToDate medical software tool in October 2025, nearly two years after OpenEvidence entered the market.

Central to OpenEvidence’s pitch is a focused source list consisting of peer-reviewed journals such as the New England Journal of Medicine and the Journal of the American Medical Association.

“OpenEvidence allows me to provide a lot of context about my patient, find information, and make decisions faster,” said Nina Singh, a medical resident at the University of California San Francisco. “It’s a really useful tool.”

Widespread appeal has helped OpenEvidence forge relationships with several hospitals and specialist clinics such as Mount Sinai Health System and Memorial Sloan Kettering Cancer Center in New York, embedding its tool within the organizations’ electronic health records.

Paul Testa, chief health informatics officer at NYU Langone, said that the hospital system sought a formal tie-up with OpenEvidence after it found clinicians were already using the tool as an “independent resource.”

“We chose to deeply integrate a clinically informed version of OpenEvidence into the care process to ensure two things: first, our clinicians can get the most from these AI tools, and second, they use them securely,” he said.

OpenEvidence has leveraged its popularity with doctors to slowly expand into other domains, including ambient documentation—note-taking during doctors’ patient interactions.

Critics have questioned whether the company’s ad-based model warrants its high valuation, while its decision to withdraw from the EU and UK earlier this year over the bloc’s AI Act has stymied its expansion into two key markets.

Mike Vernal, a partner at venture firm Conviction and an OpenEvidence investor, said that the company’s popularity among physicians represented its strongest defense against startup rivals and incumbents.

Nadler said it will also launch clinical trials in the coming weeks, partnering with researchers to target cancer and rare diseases. It plans to apply AI models to drug discovery and draw on pre-existing literature to generate novel scientific hypotheses.

“The end game is literature-based drug discovery,” Nadler said, referencing the field of data mining scientific literature for insights. “The economic value of that as a company is going to dwarf by orders of magnitude whatever we could have charged hospitals or advertisers.”

Alexander Tarashansky, the creator of Claude Science, an Anthropic platform that supports research scientists, has also joined the company to support its clinical work.

The company needs to see off competition from frontier AI companies such as OpenAI, which has also made a play for the space with ChatGPT for healthcare. Anthropic has also released healthcare tools, though it recently partnered with OpenEvidence to bring the tools to 100 low- and middle-income countries.

“The fact that doctors are adopting and using a piece of software of their own volition means there is a degree of differentiation that OpenEvidence can really lean on,” said Nworah Ayogu, a partner at investor Thrive Capital.

But analysis of OpenEvidence’s effectiveness has led to mixed results.

One study by the Mayo Clinic, an investor in the startup, found that it “provided accurate, evidence-based recommendations” in all five patient case studies that were sampled, although its impact on treatment decisions was more limited.

Other research, including a June paper published in Nature, found that it underperformed general-purpose AI models such as Google’s Gemini and OpenAI’s GPT on clinical benchmarks.

Eric Oermann, a neurosurgeon at NYU Langone, said there was a lack of research into the performance of individual AI tools and scant guidance on how to implement the tools in a clinical setting.

중국 우후, 2026년 10월 21일 /PRNewswire/ -- 미래 여행의 시작을 알리는 2026 제투어 글로벌 테크놀로지 익스피리언스 데이가 10월 20일 중국 안후이성 우후에서 공식 개막했다. 오전에는 그룹 연구개발(R&D) 센터에서 핵심 행사인 글로벌 이노베이션 콘퍼런스가 열리며 2,000여 명의 해외 게스트와 미디어, 사용자가 한자리에 모여 첨단 기술 성과와 제품 라인업, 지능형 모빌리티의 미래 청사진을 살펴다.

Yin Tongyue, Chairman of Chery Automobile Co., Ltd.

콘퍼런스에서 인퉁웨(Yin Tongyue) 체리자동차 회장은 30여 년간 이어온 혁신을 돌아보고 미래 산업 트렌드에 대한 전망을 공유했다. 그는 "AI로 자동차뿐 아니라 기업과 산업 생태계 전체를 재정의하고 있다"며 "미래의 자동차는 당신을 더 잘 이해하는 똑똑한 동반자이자, 더 큰 가능성을 담는 지능형 모빌리티 공간이 될 것"이라고 말했다. 가오신화(Gao Xinhua) CTO는 지능 시대를 위한 그룹의 기술 기반을 주제로 기조연설을 했다. 인 회장은 "체리의 기술 비전은 한 문장, 인간의 자유를 위해 더 큰 가치를 창조한다는 것"이라고 강조했다.

이번 콘퍼런스에는 스카이 돔(Sky Dome) 슈퍼컴퓨팅 센터와 스타 시(Star Sea) 빅데이터 플랫폼부터 V2G 기술, 태양광•저장•충전 일체형 솔루션까지 그룹의 첨단 기술 포트폴리오가 총망라됐다. AI 파울데이션 모델과 월드 모델의 진전, 로보택시와 AiMOGA 로봇 등 피지컬 AI의 실제 적용 사례도 공개됐다. 이들 혁신은 AI를 동력으로, 데이터를 기반으로, 여러 영역의 협업을 통해 모빌리티•에너지•일상을 아우르는 지능형 기술 생태계를 만들어 간다. R&D 센터에서는 기술 전시와 체험존이 그룹별로 순차 운영돼 참가자들이 첨단 기술을 직접 경험했다.

이러한 혁신 흐름 속에서 제투어는 사용자 니즈에 집중하며 기술 기반을 실감 나는 여행 경험으로 전환하고 있다.

제투어의 두 제품 시리즈는 도심 통근과 아웃도어 탐험을 아우른다. T 시리즈는 지능형 도심 주행의 편안함과 본격 오프로드 성능을 결합했고, 전 라인업에 C-DM 슈퍼 하이브리드를 탑재해 장거리 여행의 주행거리 불안을 덜었다. XWD 전자동 지능형 사륜구동은 7+X 원터치 지능 오프로드 모드로 도강, 자갈길, 급경사 같은 험로를 더 쉽게 극복하게 해준다. 스마트 콕핏과 지능형 주행 기술은 여정을 더 편안하고 안심되게 만든다.

G 시리즈는 프리미엄 모델을 위한 차세대 전지형 지능 아키텍처 GAIA를 기반으로, 고효율 하이브리드 시스템과 오프로드 전용 섀시를 통합했다. 여기에 지능형 인터랙션과 프리미엄 캐빈을 더해 탁월한 오프로드 성능과 럭셔리한 편안함을 하나로 묶었다.

이날 저녁 제투어는 양쯔강변에서 몰입형 비치 캠핑 환영 디너를 열었다. 제투어 차량에 내장된 고출력 V2L 기술이 마켓 전역에 전력을 공급해 야외 쿠킹과 엔터테인먼트를 가능하게 하며, 기술을 일상의 여행 경험 속에 녹여냈다. 제투어 경영진은 해외 게스트와 함께 익스피리언스 데이 시승 프로그램의 공식 시작을 알렸다.

기술은 전시장뿐 아니라 도로 위를 위해 존재한다. 기술 쇼케이스와 제품 체험, 캠핑 페어, 실제 시승에 이르기까지 이번 익스피리언스 데이는 혁신과 실제 여행 장면을 이어준다. 10월 21일 해외 게스트들은 모간산의 험준한 산악 지형으로 들어가 도강과 크로스액슬 등 다양한 노면 조건에서 제투어 차량을 직접 시승하며, 기술이 여행의 새로운 가능성을 어떻게 여는지 몸소 체험할 예정이다.

2018년 출범한 제투어는 트래블+(Travel+) 전략을 실천하며 전 세계 100여 개 국가 및 지역에 진출했고, 2,000여 개의 판매•애프터서비스 네트워크와 5,000만 명 이상의 글로벌 사용자를 보유하고 있다. 글로벌 R&D 네트워크는 유럽, 중동, 중남미, 아세안 등에 걸쳐 있다. 포트폴리오에는 라이트 오프로드 세그먼트의 T 시리즈와 프리미엄 럭셔리 오프로드 시장의 G 시리즈가 있으며, 도심 통근, 가족 로드트립, 아웃도어 캠핑, 장거리 여행 등 다양한 여행 시나리오를 아우른다.

디지털 증거는 이를 검토하는 팀보다 빠르게 증가하고 있으며, 수작업 검토 과정에서는 중요한 연관성이나 관련 증거 자료, 피해자를 의도치 않게 발견하지 못할 수 있다. 증거는 여러 기기와 파일, 시스템에 흩어져 있고, 새로운 기기와 운영체제, 증거 유형이 등장할 때마다 업무도 달라진다. 셀레브라이트의 2026년 업계 동향 설문조사 에 따르면 사건 처리에 투입되는 시간의 약 60%가 검토와 분석에 쓰이며, 응답자의 70% 이상은 여전히 증거를 수작업으로 검토하고 있다.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s Vision for Europe Runs on Plug-In Data Centers
items.summary: At Nvidia’s GTC in Berlin, Huang unveiled the company’s new plug-in data center—the DSX Pod—as the key to unlocking Europe’s AI infrastructure lag. Oh, and autonomous humanoid robotics.
items.content:
Jensen Huang outlined his vision of Europe’s future at Nvidia’s global conference in Berlin on Wednesday. It consists of robotics , AI agents, and modular data centers , with Nvidia unsurprisingly powering it all.

“To be part of this AI economy, you don’t want to just be consuming the AI. You want to be producing the AI,” he told the 4,000-strong crowd at Nvidia’s GTC. “We can do all of that here in Europe.”

The last GTC, held in San Jose, California, in March, was all about AI inference and more efficient compute. Seven months later, the focus has switched to power, agents, and physical AI. There were even some cute little Microduck robots—made by recent Nvidia acquisition Hugging Face —doing Huang’s bidding at the end of his 90-minute pitch.

Huang’s first big announcement was a modular “AI factory” called the DSX Pod. It is a “plug-and-play” option for building AI data centers, with everything arriving already assembled in a large metal container and packed with Nvidia’s latest Vera Rubin compute racks. It can be brought online in 14 days, instead of taking months or years to construct. That may come in especially handy in Europe, where infrastructure projects are notoriously slow. Huang said the DSX Pod would also slash the amount of time compute sits idle in a data center as it will come online quicker. “This is a complete transformation,” he said.

The speech, delivered at Berlin’s Tempodrom, a venue inspired by a circus tent with the lighting of a gamer’s den, veered between selling laptops and sweeping predictions, with Nvidia presented as the fundamental technology provider to every industry. At one point, two Greenpeace protesters stood up and unfurled a banner reading “Clean up your dirty business.” Huang told his security team to “Go easy” as they were marched out.

Humanoid robotics will be the “next great industry,” Huang said, arguing that Europe was well-placed to lead on it due to its manufacturing heritage. But physical AI goes way beyond robotics, Huang pointed out, explaining that even telecom operators are adding Nvidia GPUs to their cell towers. He also announced partnerships with European carmakers VW and Mercedes on AVs.

Nvidia is making a similar move in humanoid robotics, with Huang announcing the launch of a full-stack robotics platform to standardize configuration. It also plans to release a preconfigured reference robot, Agile One, available in the first quarter of next year, to help developers start building physical AI systems. “This is your great opportunity,” he said.

On model usage, Huang predicted: “Every company in the future will use both closed models as well as open models that you customize.” He showcased Nvidia’s own open-source models as hitting frontier performance once customized on an organization’s proprietary data.

He also predicted that agents would mean there will be more users of software tools than ever before, and said agents’ reasoning, iteration, and tool use are pushing token consumption and demand for computing—and Nvidia GPUs—higher.

In case the 90-minute speech was too technical, it ended with an AI-generated Eurovision song summing up what Huang had just announced. The speech was easier to follow, to be fair.
